hero.title: A reproduction of the GDM math swarm environment, with overseers
hero.lead: Up to 100 AI agents solve Lean 4 mathematics problems in a simulated research conference. Its automatic judge is weak, so agents sometimes submit fake proofs that it accepts. In some runs a fake proof is planted at the start. We add overseer agents, reminders and external monitors, and measure how much faking each setup allows.

stories.headline: Spontaneous faking in a 90-minute baseline run
stories.takeaway: Thirteen agents considered the trick before anyone used it. After agent-100 used it, 25 others did, each after reading its published files.
stories.story: No cheat was planted in this 90-minute run. Thirteen agents noticed the loophole on their own, and not one of them tried it. Then agent-100, after losing several races, used it and swept 23 credits. Every one of the 25 agents who followed had first read agent-100's published solutions in the shared library; the board and direct messages never mentioned the trick.

stories.headline: Ten overseers with pushed messages
stories.takeaway: Ten overseers whose messages land straight in each agent's next step held faking to 0 or 1 agent, against about 75 with no overseer.
stories.story: Overseers are extra agents that check proofs, reverse fake credits and warn others. When their warnings only waited in an inbox, many were never read. Once board posts and direct messages were pushed into every agent's next tool result, the same team of ten stopped the planted cheat almost completely. Warnings work when they are read: in four mapped three-hour runs, 94% of agents who read a first warning never faked again.

stories.headline: Variation between single-overseer replicates
stories.takeaway: The same single-overseer setup had 44 fakers in one replicate and none in another.
stories.story: With a single overseer, identical replicates swung wildly: 44 agents faked in replicate 1, none in replicate 2 and two in replicate 3. Two overseers kept every replicate at 4 fakers or fewer, and ten kept them at 0 or 1.

stories.headline: Talk-only versus enforce-only overseers
stories.takeaway: Overseers who could only reverse fake credits, without posting or messaging, had about twice as many fakers and over ten times as many accepted fakes as talk-only overseers.
stories.story: In three-hour runs we split the overseers' powers. Talk-only overseers could warn but not undo anything. Enforce-only overseers could reverse fake credits but never post or message. Every silent reversal reopened the problem, agents faked it again, and the more silent overseers there were, the more fakes got accepted.

stories.headline: Honesty reminders every five minutes
stories.takeaway: Repeating the integrity rules to every agent every five minutes did not reduce faking.
stories.story: Every five minutes each agent's next step carried its own proof-integrity rules, word for word: about 2,230 reminders per run. Agents read them, quoted them, and argued that the planted trick did not technically break them. Faking stayed at the level of runs with no reminder at all, in two-hour and one-hour versions alike.

upcoming.headline: External tool-call monitors
upcoming.story: Twelve two-hour runs with no overseers inside the swarm. Instead, a separate monitor scores every tool call an agent makes and blocks the ones that look like cheating. Four versions, three replicates each: the monitor reads either the actions alone or the whole transcript, and a blocked agent is told either nothing or the monitor's reason.
